pitchScripts.title: Quick WhatsApp intro
pitchScripts.body: Hey! You mentioned needing a website for the business — I know the right person. Jamie builds clean, fast sites from €200 and handles the whole thing for you. Want me to introduce you? Here's his page: {link}

pitchScripts.title: Warm email introduction
pitchScripts.body:
Hi [name],

Following up on what you said about needing a website — I work with Jamie Nisbet, a software engineer near Lisbon who builds fast, professional sites and looks after the whole thing. One-page sites start at €200; bigger builds are quoted to fit.

You can read more and reach him here: {link}

Happy to introduce you directly — just say the word.

pitchScripts.title: Face-to-face, then follow up
pitchScripts.body: "You know what — I know exactly the right person for that. Jamie builds websites and software, dead easy to deal with, and he'll quote you straight. Let me send you his link." Then text them: {link}

followUps.body: Just sent your details over to Jamie — he'll reach out in a day or two. Anything you want him to know first? Tell me and I'll pass it on.
Did Jamie manage to reach you? No rush — just making sure his message didn't land in spam. Here's his page again if it's easier: {link}
No pressure at all — if now's not the right time for the website, just say and I'll leave it. If it is, Jamie can usually have a simple one live within a couple of weeks.

objections.answer: A one-page site starts at €200, once, and works for years. Set that against the customers a business loses with no site — or a broken one. If €200 is still too much, it's probably not the right time, and that's fine.

They can, and sometimes that's the right call. The difference is the weekends spent fighting a template that still looks like one. I do it properly, once, and they get their time back. If they enjoy the DIY, don't push.

No hard sell. Just mention I'm a senior engineer who handles the whole thing for a clear fixed price — handy if their guy goes quiet or it gets technical. Leave the link; people remember it when the first option falls through.
Fine — don't chase. Ask what would make it the right time (a launch, a busy season, a rebrand) and check back then. A soft “want the link for whenever?” keeps the door open without pressure.

objections.objection: “What if it goes wrong? I'm not technical.”
objections.answer: That's the point — they never touch the technical side. I scope it, build it, and support it; they deal with one person, not an agency. And you're not on the hook for any of it either.

goodLeadSigns: They've actually said they need a website, online booking, or some software — not just "might one day".
You can name who decides and pays — the owner or a manager, not a vague "the business".
There's a reason it's now: a launch, a rebrand, a busy season, or a competitor who just went online.
They have a rough budget in mind, even if it's only "a few hundred euros".
You can give a name and a way to reach them — an email or a phone number.

faqs.a: When the client's payment reaches me — not when I send the invoice. You get 10% of what I invoice on that project, settled in one clear statement per referrer.

faqs.q: What stops two people claiming the same lead?
faqs.a: Your referral code. The first valid code logged against a new customer wins. If two codes land on the same customer, it surfaces for me to sort out fairly — so always log the lead here first.
Landing pages with a contact form, at €200 or more — quote those freely. Anything more involved (multiple pages, an app, AI, integrations), just introduce me and I'll quote it.

faqs.q: Do I have to understand the tech?
faqs.a: No. Your job is the warm intro and the simple landing-page sale. I handle scope, price, build, and support. If a customer asks something technical, point them to me.
